justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift assumption from what I infer was a recent price level around $424–425 for the underlying asset (likely SPY or a similar broad market index). At the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the prevailing price with only a small positive drift, reflecting the typical daily expected return being near zero but slightly positive over time. At the one-week horizon, I nudged the estimate up marginally to around $427, incorporating the same mild positive drift over five trading days. At one month, I extended that drift further to $430, essentially assuming trend continuation at a modest pace consistent with long-run equity returns, without projecting any major directional catalyst in either direction.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated primarily using historical volatility. For equities around this price level, daily volatility tends to run roughly 0.8–1.2%, which translates to a relatively tight band at one day. As the horizon extends to one week, uncertainty compounds with the square root of time, widening the interval to roughly plus or minus 5%. At one month, that expansion becomes more pronounced, reaching roughly plus or minus 9–10%, reflecting both the compounding of daily uncertainty and the increased probability that macroeconomic or earnings-related developments could materially shift the price. I also factored in some skew toward the downside, as markets historically exhibit heavier left tails.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden deterioration in macroeconomic data — particularly a weaker-than-expected jobs report, a surprise Federal Reserve policy shift toward renewed tightening, or an escalation in geopolitical tensions — could easily drive prices below the lower bound, especially at the one-month horizon. A credit event or liquidity shock in financial markets could produce a move well beyond the stated ranges. On the upside, a stronger-than-expected inflation print showing rapid disinflation, a dovish Fed pivot, or a surge in AI-driven earnings enthusiasm could push prices above the upper bounds.

Finally, I want to be transparent that these intervals represent my best probabilistic judgment under normal market conditions and are not derived from a live model with real-time data. My knowledge has a cutoff, meaning I cannot account for developments that occurred after that point. The intervals should be treated as rough guides rather than precise risk estimates, and any meaningful position-sizing or risk management decision should incorporate additional real-time analysis and current volatility measures.
